noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to describe the mechanism (including diagrams), giving evidence where possible, of: i the electrophilic addition of bromine and hydrogen bromide to ethene ii the electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene Use of the curly arrow notation is expected – the curly arrows should start from either a bond or from a lone pair of electrons. Knowledge of the relative stability of primary, secondary and tertiary carbocation intermediates is expected.

primer.text: Electrophiles hunt electron density, and the pi cloud is the richest target in an alkene. This note traces the two-step addition mechanism arrow by arrow: the polarised hydrogen halide case that opens onto a carbocation, and the induced dipole that lets neutral bromine attack itself. Curly arrow origins are graded, so fix them early.

lessons.title: HBr onto ethene: the two-step story
lessons.opening: The polarised hydrogen halide is the cleanest introduction to electrophilic addition. The pi bond reaches for the delta-positive hydrogen, the H-Br bond breaks to bromide, and the carbocation left behind is finished off by the bromide ion. Two curly arrows per step, none of them optional.
keyPoints: HBr is polarised H(d+)-Br(d-) because bromine is more electronegative than hydrogen.
Step one: the pi bond attacks the delta-positive hydrogen and the H-Br bond breaks to Br(-).
The intermediate is a carbocation, a carbon carrying the positive charge.
Step two: the bromide ion donates its lone pair to the carbocation, completing the addition.
Curly arrows must start from a bond or a lone pair - arrows from atoms score nothing.

low.restatement: The alkene's pi pair grabs the positive end of H-Br; bromide pops out, a carbocation forms, and the bromide then bonds to that positive carbon.
low.analogy: A magnet (H end) draws the pi pair in; the string (H-Br bond) snaps to the bromine side, and the loose end (Br-) ties itself to the leftover positive post.
low.examPointer: Show the dipole arrows on H-Br and the positive charge on the carbocation - mechanism marks are distributed across those details.

medium.restatement: Electrophilic addition proceeds through heterolytic fission of the polarised H-Br bond: the electron pair departs with bromine, so the two-step mechanism is an ionisation followed by ion pairing, and arrow origins encode exactly which electrons move.
medium.analogy: A tug-of-war where the stronger electronegative side wins the whole rope: the pair leaves with bromine, leaving carbon short-handed and charged.
medium.examPointer: With propene, name the more stable secondary carbocation and the major product 2-bromopropane - carbocation stability decides the product ratio.

check.stem: Why is the hydrogen atom of HBr described as the electrophile?

options.text: It carries a delta-positive charge from the polarised bond
options.explanation: Bromine's higher electronegativity leaves hydrogen electron-poor.

options.text: It donates electrons to the alkene
options.explanation: The hydrogen accepts electron density - donation runs the other way.
The negative end of HBr is the bromine.
HBr adds by the ionic electrophilic route.

check.stem: What happens to the polarised H-Br bond during step one of the mechanism?

options.text: It breaks heterolytically, both electrons leaving with bromine
options.explanation: The pair departs to the more electronegative atom.

options.text: It breaks homolytically to give radicals
options.explanation: No radicals appear in electrophilic addition.
The bromide must be free to attack in step two.

options.text: It transfers its electrons to hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrogen departs bonded to the pi pair instead.

check.stem: Which species attacks the carbocation in step two?

options.text: The bromide ion with its lone pair
options.explanation: Br(-) donates a pair to the positive carbon.
One addition is complete after two steps.
Hydrogen has already been delivered to the first carbon.
The bromide is the reagent's own partner.

check.stem: Where must a curly arrow start in a valid mechanism?

options.text: From a bond or a lone pair of electrons
options.explanation: Arrows track electron pairs, so they begin where pairs live.
Arrows follow electrons, never nuclei.
Charges mark destinations, not origins.
Origins must be electron sources - precision carries the mark.

check.stem: When the polarised HBr adds to propene, which product is the major one and why?

options.text: 2-bromopropane, via the more stable secondary carbocation
options.explanation: The positive charge sits on the middle carbon where alkyl groups steady it.

options.text: 1-bromopropane, via the more stable primary carbocation
options.explanation: Primary carbocations are the less stable kind.
No radical intermediates operate here.
The regioselectivity is decided, not random.

check.stem: Define the term electrophile and identify it in the HBr addition.
check.modelAnswer: An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions; in HBr addition the delta-positive hydrogen fills that role.

check.stem: Write the two steps of the HBr-plus-ethene mechanism in words, in order.
check.modelAnswer: First the pi bond attacks the delta-positive hydrogen while H-Br breaks to bromide, forming the carbocation; then the bromide ion donates its lone pair to the carbocation.

check.stem: Explain why a carbocation intermediate forms in this mechanism.
check.modelAnswer: Heterolytic fission hands the H-Br electron pair entirely to bromine, so after hydrogen bonds to one alkene carbon the other carbon is left electron-short and formally positive until bromide arrives.

check.stem: Draw the full mechanism for HBr adding to ethene, marking both curly arrow origins.
check.modelAnswer: Arrow one runs from the C=C pi bond to the delta-positive hydrogen, arrow two runs from the H-Br bond to bromine giving Br(-); after the carbocation appears, arrow three runs from the Br(-) lone pair onto the positive carbon.

lessons.title: Bromine onto ethene: the induced dipole
lessons.opening: Bromine arrives neutral and non-polar, yet the mechanism is still electrophilic addition. The secret is induction: as Br2 drifts toward the pi cloud, its electron pair is pushed to the far atom, creating a temporary delta-positive bromine that the alkene can attack.
keyPoints: Br2 is non-polar as a free molecule but polarises on approach to the electron-rich pi bond.
The induced dipole makes the near bromine delta-positive and hence electrophilic.
The pi bond attacks that polarised bromine and the Br-Br bond breaks heterolytically to Br(-).
The product of bromine addition to ethene is 1,2-dibromoethane.
The same induced-dipole logic underlies the bromine water saturation test.

low.restatement: The alkene's electron cloud pushes bromine's shared pair to the far atom, so the near bromine turns positive and gets attacked; bromide then completes the addition to give the dibromo product.
low.analogy: Hold a balloon near a wall of hair (the pi cloud) and the balloon polarises: the near side is suddenly attractive and sticks first.
low.examPointer: Say 'induced dipole' explicitly - writing that bromine 'is polar' outright contradicts the non-polar free molecule and costs the mark.

medium.restatement: Polarisability does the work: the large, diffuse bromine electron cloud distorts easily, so the pi density induces Br(d+)-Br(d-) and the addition proceeds heterolytically without any external polariser.
medium.analogy: A soft water balloon squashes against a wall - its contents shift to the far side, and the near side becomes the point of first contact.
medium.examPointer: Link the induced dipole to the decolourisation observation: consuming Br2 into the dibromo compound is exactly why bromine water fades.

check.stem: What polarises the Br-Br bond as bromine approaches an alkene?

options.text: The electron-rich pi cloud of the alkene
options.explanation: Approaching density pushes the shared pair toward the far bromine.
The induction is intrinsic to the approach, not solvent-borne.

options.text: The hydrogen atoms on the alkene
options.explanation: Hydrogens are not the polarising agent here.
Light initiates radical reactions, not this ionic addition.

check.stem: Which description of the polarised Br2 species is correct?

options.text: Near bromine delta-positive, far bromine delta-negative
options.explanation: Electron density is pushed away from the approaching atom.

options.text: Near bromine delta-negative, far bromine delta-positive
options.explanation: The push runs away from the alkene, so the near end is positive.
One atom takes the deficit, not both.
Polarisation is the entire mechanism's trigger.

check.stem: What is the organic product when bromine adds to ethene?

options.explanation: One bromine on each alkene carbon - di-substituted.
Two bromine atoms enter; both must appear in the product.
No oxygen participates in bromine addition.
Carbon count is unchanged at two.

check.stem: How does the Br-Br bond break during electrophilic addition to ethene?

options.text: Heterolytically, giving Br(-) and the polarised electrophile
options.explanation: Both electrons leave with the departing bromide.
Radical chemistry belongs to UV substitution routes.
Both atoms join the product, so the bond must break first.
The departing species carries one electron pair, making a single negative ion.

check.stem: Why does the bromine water test also work through this mechanism?

options.text: The alkene induces the same dipole and consumes Br2 into a dibromo product, bleaching the reagent
options.explanation: Consumption of bromine is the visible endpoint.

options.text: Bromine water is ionic and reacts by substitution
options.explanation: The addition pathway, not substitution, consumes the reagent.
Water is the solvent; manganate does the oxidising.
The test works in the dark with alkenes.

check.stem: Define an induced dipole in the context of bromine addition.
check.modelAnswer: An induced dipole is the temporary charge separation created when the alkene's electron density pushes the Br-Br shared pair toward the far bromine, making the near atom delta-positive.

check.stem: State the equation for bromine adding to ethene, with the product name.
check.modelAnswer: CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> CH2BrCH2Br, the addition giving 1,2-dibromoethane.

check.stem: Explain why bromine, though non-polar, still participates in electrophilic addition.
check.modelAnswer: Electrophilic character does not require a permanent dipole: the pi cloud induces one on approach, and the induced delta-positive bromine behaves exactly like any other electrophile.

check.stem: Propene is treated with bromine water. Name the organic product and state the observation.
check.modelAnswer: Addition places bromine across the double bond to give 1,2-dibromopropane, and the orange bromine water decolourises as the reagent is consumed.

glossary.definition: A two-step reaction in which an electron-seeking species is attacked by a pi bond and the reagent splits across the double bond.
The positively charged carbon intermediate formed after the pi bond has bonded the first fragment.
Bond breaking in which both bonding electrons depart with one atom, producing ions.
The temporary polarisation of a non-polar molecule caused by nearby electron density.
